headline: Terns Working Nervous Water Off Sankaty — Albies Are Around, Just Not Committed
subhead: Bluefish are the sure thing this week from Craigville to Osterville while the albies feed on bait too small for most boxes and bonito stage just to the east.
body_markdown:
There's been a good tell running off Sankaty most mornings this week — terns stacking tight and dropping hard into slicks of nervous water, then peeling off before the bait even breaks the surface. That's the signature right now: fish are there, they're working, but they're not committing to anything big or obvious. Get close enough and you can see why. The bait balled up under those birds is tiny — bay anchovies and rice-grain silversides, not the fall peanut bunker everyone's hoping shows up. That's the whole story of the albie bite in Nantucket Sound this week: present, active, and stubborn.

We flagged the bonito potential building a few days back on the back of the warm water sitting over the Cape and Islands, and that's exactly the direction this is heading. Block Island and Point Judith got run over with bonito this week, and that push doesn't stop at the Sound line — it walks west. Give it several days to two weeks and there's a real chance those fish show up hard around Great Point and the deeper cuts off Nantucket Shoals, the same water where albies are already teasing the fleet. Worth watching the outer edges — Great Point rip on the last of the ebb, and the deeper humps off the Shoals where the bait tends to stage before it gets pushed onto the flats.

The sure thing this week isn't the albies, it's the bluefish. Between Craigville and Osterville the blues have been dependable — mid-Sound structure, drifting bucktails and small metal (Deadly Dicks, half-ounce Kastmasters) through bait schools on the moving tide, with black sea bass mixing in on the same structure for boats working bottom rigs with squid strips. That's the everyday catch right now, and it's been steady enough that it's worth building a morning around even when the more glamorous stuff is being difficult.

On the albie front, the fix is going smaller, not louder. Standard Albie Snax and 3-inch epoxy jigs are getting refused when the fish are locked onto anchovy-sized bait. Size 2 bay anchovy flies, small Deceivers, and the smallest Albie Snax in the box — the 2.5-inch, not the standard — have been the difference for guys willing to downsize. Same with spin gear: a 1/2-ounce epoxy jig retrieved fast and erratic beats a slow strip almost every time when the bait's this small. Best water has been off Sankaty on the ebb and around Great Point where the rip concentrates that fine bait against the current line. Patience matters here — these are pods that show, feed for a few minutes, and go quiet, so working a milk run of known rips beats parking on one spot and waiting.

Striped bass are still in that in-between stage the whole region's dealing with — around, catchable, but not yet grouped up tight enough to blitz. Monomoy and the rips off Chatham have had scattered bass on the last two hours of the ebb, mostly on soft plastics — 5-inch white paddletails on light jigheads — worked along the current seams where the sandbars break up the flow. Nothing to write home about yet, but the moon's building toward full over the next week, which means more water moving through those cuts and more bait getting pinned against structure. That's usually the trigger that turns a scattered bass pattern into a real one, so the next week to ten days is worth watching closely, especially around Monomoy Point and the Chatham inlet on a hard SW blow that stacks bait against the beach.

Fluke are doing what they do this time of year — softening, but not done. Horseshoe Shoal and the deeper channel edges around the Sound have still been giving up keeper fish on white Gulp paired with 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom on the last of the incoming when the water's had a chance to warm through the day. It's not a bent-rod-every-drift kind of bite anymore, but there's enough there to justify a stop before the season shifts fully to fall species.

Looking at the next few days: expect the bluefish to keep producing without much drama, expect the albies to stay frustrating until either the bait size changes or more fish push in behind the bonito wave building to the east, and keep an eye on Monomoy and Chatham as the moon fills and the tides get more current behind them. If there's only one window to fish this week, the ebb tide at Great Point or off Sankaty in the first hour of light is the one — that's when the bird activity has been tightest and the water's had all night to settle clean. Bring the small stuff regardless of what you're targeting; right now in the Sound, the fish are picky, not absent.
